name: Jaw implants

card.summary: Implants placed along the angle and body of the lower jaw to widen or define it; used in facial gender surgery and cosmetic work, with little outcome research behind the forum hype.
card.aka: mandible angle implants, gonial angle implants, jawline implants
card.note: Published outcome research is limited; users and reviews raise questions about design, size and how natural the result looks.

quick.overview:
Jaw implants, sometimes called mandibular angle or gonial implants, are solid shapes of silicone, porous polyethylene or PEEK placed over the lower jawbone to add width or definition at the angle and body of the jaw. In published literature they appear mainly in facial gender-affirming surgery, where augmentation of the mandibular angle and body is described as a masculinising option.

In looksmaxxing communities they are discussed as an alternative to bimax and genioplasty, with arguments about implant design, size, body fat and how natural the result looks. Outcome research on cosmetic jaw implants is thin.
quick.mechanism: An implant is placed against the bone through an incision, usually inside the mouth, and sits under the soft tissue so that the lower face contour looks wider or squarer. Some designs are custom-made from CT scans.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include a bloated or unnatural look when implants are too large or the underlying structure is mismatched, soft-tissue sagging after removal, infection and displacement, though complications are described as minimal in one gender-affirming surgery review. Outcome data are limited.

lead: Jaw implants are manufactured shapes, usually of silicone or porous polyethylene, placed against the outer surface of the lower jaw (the mandible) to add width, squareness and definition to the lower face. They are also called mandibular angle, gonial angle or jawline implants.[1][7] People who want a stronger or wider jawline use them to change the outline of the lower face without cutting the jawbone, and they are often paired with a chin implant or a sliding genioplasty so that chin and jaw read as one continuous contour.[4]

The procedure has a clinical literature of its own, which describes two basic implant types for aesthetic augmentation of the jaw angles, standard and custom, and discusses technique and ways to avoid common complications.[7] A prospective study of 116 solid silicone implants reported low infection rates and high patient satisfaction, while a case series of implant movement and muscle displacement has urged surgeons to preserve the soft-tissue sling around the angle of the jaw.[7] The best-known related setting is facial gender-affirming surgery, where a review of lower jaw recontouring describes reducing or augmenting the angle, body and chin and reports minimal complications.[1]

On looksmax.org, jaw implants are discussed as a lower-downtime alternative or complement to bone surgery such as bimaxillary surgery, with long-running debates about implant design, size, body fat and whether the underlying skeleton suits an implant.[3] Published outcome research on cosmetic jaw implants remains small, and much of the discussion rests on individual before-and-after reports.[7]

angle.text: The implant adds volume along the outer edge of the jaw, which changes the width and outline of the lower face. People use it to build a more defined jawline, often together with a chin implant or genioplasty so the contour reads as continuous.

paras: A jaw implant is a solid or semi-solid shape that sits against the outer surface of the lower jawbone. Different designs target the gonial angle at the back corner of the jaw, the body along the side, or an extended shape that wraps both; some are made as custom pieces from CT scans of the individual patient.[7] Surgeons usually place them through an incision inside the mouth so that there is no visible scar, creating a pocket over the bone for the implant.[4]

A 2019 review of mandibular angle implants by the surgeon Barry Eppley describes the two basic types of implant used for aesthetic augmentation of the jaw angles, the goals of augmentation, how the implants are placed with attention to avoiding common complications, and when standard versus custom implants are indicated.[7]

The anatomical logic is that a wider, sharper lower face reads as more masculine or more defined. An overview of facial feminisation surgery notes that male jawlines extend from the chin at a wider angle and end in a sharper corner at the back than female jawlines, and that chins in men tend to be longer, wider and squarer.[5] Many looksmaxxing discussions of the jawline use the same vocabulary of angle, width and squareness.

Materials discussed for chin implants, which forum users apply by analogy to jaw implants, include silicone, which is smooth and flexible, does not bond to tissue and is easy to remove; porous polyethylene (Medpor), into which tissue grows, anchoring it and helping resist infection but making removal harder; and ePTFE, which is flexible, porous and held with titanium screws.[4] Wikipedia notes that silicone can shift or buckle and, in some cases, cause bone resorption where it contacts the mandible.[4]

For the jaw angle specifically, a 1996 report from oral and maxillofacial surgeons described a large-pore polyethylene implant used in patients with severe facial deformities and previous surgery, presenting four cases with very satisfactory aesthetic results and recommending the approach when indications are strictly observed.[7] Later series have concentrated on solid silicone.

Bone-based approaches include orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery, in which the upper jaw, lower jaw or both are cut, moved and fixed; it is mainly used for bite and jaw-structure problems and can also be considered for aesthetics, with software used to predict the post-operative appearance.[6] Sliding genioplasty cuts a horseshoe-shaped piece from the lower chin border and moves it forward or back, fixing it with a plate and screws.[4] Non-surgical options for the lower face include hyaluronic acid or calcium hydroxyapatite fillers, which are temporary, while permanent free silicone injections have fallen out of favour because of migration and inflammation.[4]

Facial gender-affirming literature treats jaw work as one element of a package that may include the chin, cheeks and forehead. Wikipedia reports that the jaw can be reshaped by reduction surgery through the mouth and that the masseter muscle can be reduced to make the jaw look narrower, and that surgeons began developing the field in the early 1980s, notably Douglas Ousterhout after a request in 1982.[5]

A review of lower jaw recontouring in facial gender-affirming surgery describes augmentation of the angle, body and chin with implants, fat or bone, reports minimal complications and says more outcome research is needed.[1]

A prospective study from Al-Jandan and Marei, published in 2018, followed 58 patients (56 women and 2 men) who received bilateral solid silicone mandibular angle implants, 116 implants in all, for at least six months. In the abstract, 96 implants had no complications, 5 (4.3 percent) became infected and 16 (13.8 percent) were displaced, and three patients without complications (6 percent) were dissatisfied with their final appearance. The authors concluded that infection and displacement rates were low and satisfaction high.[8][7]

A 2010 report by Bastidas and Zide, titled 'The treachery of mandibular angle augmentation', described five patients with complications after angle augmentation with silicone or porous implants, including implant movement and displacement of the masseter muscle, one of which needed revision through a modified Risdon approach. The authors advocated maintaining the pterygomasseteric sling during placement.[7]

A retrospective CT study of cosmetic-surgery foreign bodies in the maxillofacial region catalogued how such materials appear on imaging as incidental findings and did not assess outcomes.[2] Dental, corticobasal or subperiosteal jaw implants, such as 3D-printed titanium frameworks for tooth replacement, address chewing function in people with bone loss and are a separate field from cosmetic contouring.[9]

General risks described for chin and jaw implants include swelling, haematoma and temporary lip numbness or weakness, with less common problems such as infection, implant displacement, bony changes and nerve injury; surgeon experience is described as reducing these.[4] Bone-cutting procedures in facial feminisation list injury to the mental nerve, damage to tooth roots, infection and non-union.[5] Orthognathic surgery is reported to carry infection rates of up to 7 percent and temporary numbness that usually recovers within about three months, with rare permanent nerve damage.[6]
Forum users add concerns specific to appearance: an implant that is too large or does not fit the underlying bone can look bloated, and removal may not return the soft tissue to its earlier state.[3]

Jaw implants are a regular topic on looksmax.org, where threads compare them with bimaxillary surgery, ask whether a given face is a suitable candidate, share early post-operative photos and discuss surgeons and travel for surgery.[3] Participants frequently argue over whether disappointing results come from implant design or from the size chosen, with some advocating more conservative augmentation.[3]

One thread asks whether being heavier at the time of surgery changes the final look and whether leaning down later resolves it; one reply states that a short or recessed mandible can make an implant on the side look bloated.[3] These are community opinions rather than published findings.

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes one of the first cases in what becomes orthognathic jaw surgery.[6]
Jaw osteotomies develop; Hugo Obwegeser later popularises the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy.[6]
Douglas Ousterhout is asked to operate on a trans woman patient, beginning his development of facial feminisation procedures including jaw and chin work.[5]
Surgeons report large-pore polyethylene implants for mandibular angle augmentation in patients with severe deformities.[7]
Bastidas and Zide report five cases of complications after angle augmentation and urge preservation of the pterygomasseteric sling.[7]
A prospective series of 116 solid silicone angle implants reports 4.3 percent infection and 13.8 percent displacement.[8][7]
Reviews of mandibular angle implants and of lower jaw recontouring in facial gender-affirming surgery are published.[1][7]

lore.intro: Jaw implants are discussed on forums as a way to widen or define the lower face, with recurring debates about design versus size, about which skeletal structures suit an implant, and about how they compare with bimaxillary surgery.[3]

claims.claim: Being a little overweight at the time of surgery does not change the final implant result once weight is lost.
claims.believers: A poster asks whether the effect of body fat is temporary and a reply argues that a small amount of extra fat does not change the end result.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies were identified that examine body fat and the appearance of cosmetic jaw implants.

claims.claim: Jaw implants look bloated or unnatural on people with a short or recessed mandible.
claims.believers: A reply in the thread says that if the mandible is short or recessed, adding material at the side can look unnatural, like being fat.[3]
claims.experts: No published trial has compared implant and bone-based jaw changes for appearance; a review of gender-affirming jaw contouring says outcome research is still needed.[1]

claims.claim: Poor jaw implant results usually come from oversizing rather than from implants as a concept.
claims.believers: Some forum posters say that drastic changes, not the implant itself, produce unnatural results and that conservative sizing avoids this.[3]
claims.experts: The literature on gender-affirming jaw contouring reports minimal complications but does not compare sizes or designs, and calls for more outcome data.[1]

claims.claim: Implants are a cheaper, lower-downtime route to a stronger jawline than bone surgery.
claims.believers: Forum participants describe implants as an option for people who want a changed jaw outline without bimaxillary surgery, and share early post-operative photos and surgeon recommendations.[3]
claims.experts: Orthognathic surgery is mainly used for bite and jaw-structure problems, with healing of about 2 to 6 weeks initially and 2 to 4 months for full bone healing.[6] No published study compares aesthetic outcomes of implants with bone surgery.

claims.claim: Silicone implants are low-risk once placed correctly.
claims.believers: Users cite surgeons and published series describing low infection and good satisfaction.[3][8]
claims.experts: The 2018 series reported 4.3 percent infection and 13.8 percent displacement of implants and 6 percent dissatisfaction, which the authors called low; a 2010 report describes complications including implant movement and masseter displacement.[7][8]

claims.claim: Porous polyethylene anchors better than silicone, but is harder to remove if the result disappoints.
claims.believers: Forum discussion of chin and jaw implants frequently contrasts silicone, which is easy to remove, with porous implants that tissue grows into.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes silicone as easy to remove but able to shift, and porous polyethylene as anchored by tissue ingrowth but much harder to remove.[4]
